utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is case number IT-94-2-PT, the Prosecutor versus Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If it please the Court, Dirk Ryneveld, along with Bill Smith, for the Prosecution this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Howard Morrison for the accused Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Morrison. Does your letters patent as one of Her Majesty's counsel not convey -- carry here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, sometimes it does and sometimes it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It depends which robes you have with you, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, it depends which ones I'm able to bring, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would it be appropriate to treat this as a Status Conference so the time runs, Mr. Morrison?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there anything you want to raise under the relevant Rule in relation to your client's detention or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: No, not directly relating to the client's detention. The only thing I seek to say, and I don't say it with any sense of criticism or even particular urgency, but the words "amended indictment" come to mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. I've got that on my list too. Mr. Ryneveld will no doubt tell us how he is excluding unnecessary charges. But are there any matters you want to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: The only matter apart from the issue which Your Honour has raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Well, the whole of this Status Conference was called in order to try and bring to a head one way or another your client's application. Mr. Ryneveld, what about the amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. I'm acutely aware of the fact that I indicated to Your Honour last date that we were in the process of working on that. I must tell you that we have not finalised that process. I am awaiting the return of Mr. Groome, as you know, who is counsel on this case, who is still on his honeymoon. I anticipate that we will be finalising that matter in the very near future and hope to have an amended indictment available shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It probably will fall on completely deaf ears in the Office of the Prosecutor, but I hope that this current style of indictment will not be followed in this case. It would be such a good idea to start off chronologically and end up with charges rather than with the charges and then telling us what it's all about later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour will probably have noted a difference in formatting, if we want to call it, in terms of which sections of the indictment proceed and follow each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's almost totally confusing, if I may say so, and it resulted in another case with which you are concerned in a suggestion by the media, who are necessarily ignorant of procedures, that you had downplayed a particular matter because it was at the end of the indictment instead of at the beginning. So you can see that it doesn't work terribly well from the OTP's point of view either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, I certainly appreciate Your Honour's observations, which I shall convey to those who have given me my instructions. In any event, I can assure the Court and my learned friend that this matter will be given priority. You should also be aware, Your Honour, that my understanding is that although I am still on record as senior trial attorney, my understanding is that I may not be following this matter. But I have -- before handing this matter over to whoever follows me, I will ensure that an amended indictment is in their hands rather than waiting for someone else to get up to speed on the file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You see, this case started off with what was proudly proclaimed by counsel who was in it as having a record number of counts, 80. It would be a good idea if it perhaps it went down on the record as having the least necessary number of counts. You can convey that one too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I shall, and I can tell the Court that I'm personally persuaded that this matter needs to be streamlined and shall be streamlined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Well, now, in relation to this application by the defendant to be released because of the circumstances of his arrest, I have to make it very clear to you both that I am not going to draft any agreement between you as to the basis on which it proceeds. If there's one thing I have learnt as a judge of some 20 years standing now is that you can never force upon the parties the terms of an agreed issue. Four years in the commercial list was enough to persuade me of that. But it seems to me that the differences between you in the documents that have come in so far are quite unnecessary. Facts can be agreed without admission for the sole purposes of deciding an issue of law. The issue of law, I think, is a sensitive one. It has to be dealt with so that it produces an issue in this case. Whatever happens, we are not going to write a textbook on the law of unlawful detention or arrest. It just is very silly to do so. Most of the cases who talk about requiring the involvement, to use a weasel word, of the Prosecution in the illegality concede, however, that if there is some illegality in the circumstances of the arrest or the detention which makes a fair trial impossible, it doesn't matter how it happened or where it happened or by whom, and that, I think, we can put to one side, because there's no suggestion anywhere that that is the case here. So we come down to what I hope I try to define in the document that I prepared for you: Does the Prosecution have to be involved? And I accept that there's a certain ambiguity in the word "involved." And if it's not the Prosecution personally, is SFOR its agent for the purposes of the arrest or detention? Now, the wording of the document I have put was done very hurriedly after a 36-hour trip back from my hometown and probably suffering from some degree of jet lag, so I don't think that there should be any particular value placed upon it. I've put words in square brackets because I couldn't at that stage think of anything better, and I hope that between you, you will be able to come to some agreement. If you can't, and I'm not criticising anybody if you can't, but if you can't, then I'm afraid, Mr. Morrison, we'll just simply say, what do you want to do next, which would, I should think, enter into the quagmire of getting assistance from SFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's exactly what we are all seeking to avoid. I understand from my learned friend, Mr. Ryneveld, that the draft which we've kindly supplied, bearing in mind the two documents that you received from us, and that the -- as I understood it, and it didn't come directly from my learned friend Mr. Ryneveld but from Mr. Groome, one of the problems was that it was perceived that by agreeing to my draft there was some degree of compromise by the OTP. Well, I don't see it like that. It's not a question of compromise; it's simply a question of what are the issues that the Court has to determine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But you'll notice that I have tried to put it in the most general of terms rather than specifying the particular conduct involved. I've also tried very hard to avoid identifying where it occurred, because I thought that threw up false issues really. So if you could proceed along those lines, and it's only very much a suggested draft, and see if you can come to some agreement and the agreement is reached without prejudice or without admissions, however you would like to place it, so that we can determine this. It may be that the Trial Chamber will come to the conclusion that international law is completely different from any other law and that any illegality, no matter where it happens, is sufficient. I don't know. It's a very complicated problem. But if we can get that issue determined so that if you succeeded on that, you don't need SFOR, then we'll go ahead with it. If you do need SFOR, or if you need the OTP even more so, then there will be other stages. Now, I think there's been a very common misconception as to what happened in Todorovic, a misconception mainly by the NATO countries, as far as I can see, because I thought that the judgement was reasonably clear. All that NATO was asked to do in that case was not to reveal its own criminal conduct, if there was any; it was to assist the accused to know what part the Prosecution had played in the arrest. And that seemed to me to be a very, very narrow issue and it was not ordered because of some magical quality that SFOR may obtain. Indeed, it's rather difficult to know what its legal personality is. It was simply that there was a source from which it was on the cards likely that there would be information, if there was any information, about the part played by the Prosecution in the arrest or detention. So the proceedings against SFOR were not in order to make it guilty of something but simply to find out what part, if any, the Prosecution played in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the way I perceived it, and the only reason one doesn't want, if one can avoid, to go down that avenue straight away, is that no matter how much Your Honour and others, with respect, may perceive it, it's plainly not the way that NATO perceives it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I know. It's a very emotional thing from their point of view. I can understand their emotions. But it was an unfortunate result that they took the course that they did. There were no arrests for six months after that, which struck me as being childish in the extreme, but nevertheless part of the reality of the circumstances in which this Tribunal has to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can suggest this: I don't know how my learned friend is fixed for the next hour or so. He hasn't got a very busy schedule, I'm sure. But if he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He has to be back here tomorrow for another event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: He can be back here tomorrow. But if I have an unequivocal undertaking that he will supply the coffee and the sticky buns we will sit down now and sort this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well then, if you can do that. And if you can come to some agreement. It can be done in writing. We can file it and we'll have a look at to see if there's any problem about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: It may well be, given the nature of this issue, that rather than file a draft, we simply submit a draft, because that seems to take rather a long time if we go through the whole process of filing. I don't know go I'm circumventing some essential procedure by suggesting that. If I am, no doubt I won't be allowed to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. Filing simply means that the Registry undertakes service of any document on the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Precisely. If we can just put it in the hands of your assistant, Gabrielle McIntyre, then that seems to be the fastest way of resolving any issues and I would like to walk out of this building today having got it sorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I'll be here all day on other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I may just make these comments now, and that is that the Prosecution is anxious to resolve and litigate the legal issue as identified by Your Honour. We're just apprehensive that we do not want to expand the proceedings into anything beyond the initial issue to which we agreed, was: What remedies exist? And we would not want this to turn into a fact-finding exercise per se. And my only concern with the wording of point 2 is that it perhaps contemplates some form of fact-finding exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. Point 2 was intended to say that except in the case where it can be demonstrated that the Prosecutor, for example, directed the -- or pleaded with SFOR to do something illegal, what is the relationship between SFOR and the Prosecution in relation to detention and arrest? Now, in Todorovic, that was gone into in great detail from documents, including one which Mr. Morrison may have some trouble with, and that's the statement that SFOR does not regard itself in any way as obliged to do anything on behalf of the Prosecution. In fact, it doesn't feel obliged to do anything that -- unless it stumbles over a person indicted somewhere in the street, they can arrest him. That was a statement made some years ago, and one hopes that they have got over that particular view. But that's what I meant. There is documentary stuff which -- and we would refer simply to what's in the Todorovic decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And Your Honour would anticipate or envisage that this be a purely legal exercise based on submissions as opposed to the calling of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, yes. We are not going to make any finding of agency in this case unless Mr. Morrison has got some evidence, which I would have expected him to put in the motion anyway, and it's not there, that the Prosecution in some way, outside the ordinary event, assured - I'm sorry - asked SFOR to do something illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That having been clarified, I think I can perhaps shorten proceedings by indicating to Your Honour that I would be content with the questions as formulated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. Please don't do that. There was recently an application for leave to appeal against a decision in which I participated in, which I had drafted and what I thought would be an acceptable part of the indictment, and I was accused of taking over the role of the Prosecution. I'm not drafting anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Having said that, I suppose I have to supply the sticky buns and we will attempt to resolve this matter and get back to Your Honour before close of business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And after all, another thing from having been a judge for over 20 years, you do learn that counsel know their cases better than Judges and that they are better to be able to formulate the issues as they see them and as they want them to be resolved. Now, when I talk about in some way and by aiding and abetting, I'm using very generalised wording. I think you could probably do better between you about that. I don't want there to be a criticism later in the Appeals Chamber, if it gets there, that we have forced upon you something which was imperfect. So I'm saying it very clearly now. I accept that my somewhat jet-lagged attempt to suggest something to bring this to a resolution is probably very imperfect, but it was an attempt to show that this could be resolved by agreed facts made without admission, agreed without admission. Now, is there anything else that we can deal with at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, provided that the court staff, by which I include all the interpreters and court reporting, don't go away for a picnic or something, if you need to come back, we might be able to arrange a further hearing, but hopefully you can do it on paper without one. All right. Well, thank you very much for your attendance, and I hope that you can come to some resolution. I'll adjourn now.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
